# Smokeless powder and high-explosive shells (`smokeless_powder_high_explosive_shell`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs nitric_acid, sulphuric_acid; helped by nitroglycerin_dynamite, rifling_minie_breechloader, synthetic_dyes
- Core idea: Nineteenth-century chemists developed smokeless propellants that left much less smoke and solid residue than black powder. French service adoption in the 1880s was an important step. High-explosive shell fillings were a separate development. A propellant burns rapidly to produce expanding gas, while a high explosive detonates with a shock wave. The two innovations changed battlefield visibility and the effects of artillery. Factory disasters and the deterioration of stored materials accompanied the expansion of these industries.
- Pitfalls:
  - Early guncotton decomposed and blew up factories for forty years; safe manufacture was the invention, and it is industrial chemistry, not workshop craft
  - Confusing burning (propellants) with detonation (bursting charges); a detonating charge in a gun barrel destroys the gun
  - Smokeless propellants need stronger steel barrels than black powder
  - Assuming it can be made in an early modern setting; it needs concentrated acids in bulk and close temperature control
- History: europe: 1846 – Schönbein's guncotton; 1884 – Vieille's Poudre B, used in the Lebel rifle of 1886; 1887 – Nobel's ballistite; 1889 – British cordite; late 19th c. – picric acid shell fillings adopted in France (melinite) and later Britain (lyddite); 1897 – French 75 mm quick-firing gun; 1902 – Germany adopts TNT for shells; east_asia: 1890s – Japanese Shimose powder (picric acid) used in 1904–1905; global: 1914–1918 – artillery with high-explosive shells causes the majority of battle casualties
- Read:
  - G. I. Brown, The Big Bang: A History of Explosives (1998)
  - Jack Kelly, Gunpowder: Alchemy, Bombards, and Pyrotechnics (2004)
